title: Peguis First Nation members, including chief and councillor, try to oust CFS leader
summary: Anger and frustration with Peguis Child and Family Services came to a head Thursday when the First Nation's chief and band members tried to enter the organization's building, and a chain was attached…

image.caption: Two men attach a chain to the doors of Peguis First Nation's child and family services building in Manitoba's Interlake area Thursday. (Prabhjot Singh Lotey/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

Anger and frustration with Peguis Child and Family Services came to a head Thursday when the First Nation's chief and band members tried to enter the organization's building, and a chain was attached to its doors in an apparent attempt to break them open.
Band members later attached chain to building's doors in apparent bid to pull them off

Anger and frustration with Peguis Child and Family Services came to a head Thursday when the First Nation's chief and band members tried to enter the organization's building to oust its executive director and lawyer, and a chain was attached to its doors in an apparent attempt to break them open.

"They're accountable to our children and our families, and they haven't been. So, we've asked questions. We've been patient — 2½ years I've been at this. Haven't made any progress. So, we're forced to do this," Chief Stan Bird said outside the office.

Bird alleges CFS leadership have repeatedly denied the band council information. He says the council is excluded from decision-making over how the agency addresses concerns, how its money is managed, and who is hired or gets services.

More than a dozen people joined Bird and Coun. Dennis Cameron on the on-reserve CFS property in Manitoba's Interlake area in the early evening, after council held a community meeting at the local hall, which was attended by more than 50 people.

Some brought forward long-standing concerns about conflict of interest at the agency and a lack of communication, transparency and external oversight. Some also questioned decisions and spending surrounding gatherings and travel.
Peguis First Nation is about 150 kilometres north of Winnipeg. As of October 2025, 222 children were in Peguis CFS care, an open letter to members stated.

At the end of the meeting, Bird announced — without an apparent council vote — that at the community's request, they were removing the agency's executive director, Clemene Hornbrook, and lawyer Earl Stevenson from their positions that day.
After the meeting, Bird and some band members drove from the community hall to the nearby CFS building to remove Hornbrook and Stevenson from the property. It's unclear if they were inside.
Band members prepare to attach a chain to the doors of the on-reserve CFS building after backing up a truck. (Rosanna Hempel/CBC)
The building's exterior front doors were locked, and a piece of wood was fastened across the interior doors, preventing them from being opened. People banged on the doors and windows.
One band member repeatedly shouted, "You're fired."
"I'll pull my truck up," the man said shortly thereafter.
Community members then worked to back a truck up to the doors and thread a chain attached to the truck through exterior door handles.
Soon after, several RCMP officers from the Fisher Branch detachment showed up to keep the peace, a police spokesperson said, and negotiated with Bird as his supporters listened and shouted.
Manitoba RCMP confirmed Friday they didn't arrest anyone, and said no children were inside the building at the time.
It's unclear whether Bird and his council have the authority to fire Hornbrook or Stevenson.
When asked whether he endorsed band members attaching a chain to the door, Bird replied, "No, that's a bit drastic, I think. But I think it was more to get their attention."
CBC News asked to speak to Hornbrook on Friday and requested a comment from Peguis CFS but did not hear back before publication. Stevenson could not be reached.
Peguis First Nation members try to oust CFS leader
The on-reserve Peguis CFS office is currently in lockdown due to the "small protest," the organization said in a news release posted on social media early Friday evening.
"The agency is an essential service provider to Peguis members and wants to ensure ... members that programs and services will continue as normal," the release said.
It said Peguis CFS remains focused on the community's children and families, adding that all of the on-reserve children in its care are being looked after by family members.
For off-reserve kids, that proportion is 83 per cent, the release said.
'There's a better way to do things'

Earlier, at the community meeting, a woman who can't be identified so as not to identify her great-grandchildren addressed the crowd in an emotional speech. She said her six great-grandchildren were recently apprehended and taken away from the First Nation without consulting extended family.
"I'm angry. There's a better way to do things," she later told CBC.
"You would have thought CFS here would have ... known what to do instead of just, you know, getting outsiders to come and pick up these kids and take them away."
Her grandson and his wife were experiencing addictions, the woman said. She argued that other family members, including herself, were willing to look after the children.
A chain attached to the door. The chief says the move was 'a bit drastic.' (Rosanna Hempel/CBC)

Peguis CFS was created under a co-ordination agreement between the federal and provincial governments under Bill C-92. That bill, passed in 2019, gave First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities the authority to take over child welfare in their communities.
In January 2023, Peguis First Nation became the first Indigenous community in the province to sign a co-ordination agreement, and the third in Canada.
The agreement is coming up for a five-year renewal, and Bird says band members want its ongoing problems to stop.
Based on the great-grandmother's understanding, Peguis assuming authority over child welfare services was meant to keep the First Nation's children on reserve.
Chief Stan Bird and band members protest before police arrive. (Rosanna Hempel/CBC)
"That's like residential school. That's why I was taken away," she said of the current process.
Bird has previously alleged the board is operating illegally because its directors were not formally appointed through a band council resolution after their terms lapsed.

items: Once-lauded Peguis First Nation child welfare agreement a failure, should be ended: chief

blocks.text: The First Nation's child welfare act was drafted before he was elected in 2023. Bird claimed it was done without adequate community consultations.
"Our people were not consulted when it was being developed. So, how can it be our law?"
Bird wants the act reviewed and the agency investigated.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rosanna Hempel is a multiplatform journalist with a background in biology and forestry. She has been with CBC Manitoba since 2023, covering everything from extreme weather, health and housing to issues affecting Indigenous communities. She previously worked at CJOB/Global Winnipeg, where she was part of a team recognized by the Radio Television Digital News Association for its coverage of the 2023 Carberry bus crash.
